verdicts.why: No finding states the advisory's mechanism. The advisory is a two-step chain ending in revocation at the CA: an attacker reads a victim cert's body/authority.id/external_id, POSTs a DUPLICATE Certificate row to /api/1/certificates/upload (no uniqueness on body/serial/external_id), and then calls PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke on that duplicate, where the handler's creator-bypass (lemur/certificates/views.py:1675 'if g.current_user != cert.user' skips CertificatePermission) and the empty-endpoints check both pass, so service.revoke() revokes the REAL production certificate at the CA using the authority's stored credentials. Across all 56 findings the word 'revoke' appears only incidentally inside a CORS finding (R39); nothing mentions the revoke endpoint, the duplicate row, the missing uniqueness constraint, or the creator bypass. Closest is R29, 'Certificate upload endpoint lacks authorization gate present in creation endpoint' (views.py:200/650): it correctly observes that CertificatesUpload only checks StrictRolePermission while CertificatesList POST also checks AuthorityPermission(data['authority'].id, roles) at line 529. That is one precondition the advisory cites, but R29 is a different defect as stated: different endpoint (upload only), different operation (creating a cert record under an authority you lack rights to), and a different attacker outcome ('upload certificates to authorities they lack permission for'). It never reaches the revoke path, so it does not describe the arbitrary-revocation defect; fixing exactly what R29 reports would leave the row-based revoke authorization intact. R01/R04 (no authorization on GET /certificates/{id}) and R34 (coarse is_admin_or_global_cert_issuer flag) are separate authorization weaknesses on read/create, not this defect.
